searchDocs.content: </> ContainerService:Take( container: ContainerData, holder: ItemHolder, destination: Inventory, quantity: number? ) → TransferResult Move quantity out of one of the container's slots into destination. Returns what actually moved. The old signature returned(took_anything, remaining) and recomputed the remainder from three separate quantities at the call site; TransferResult carries both, named.

searchDocs.title: TakeFor​
searchDocs.content: </> ContainerService:TakeFor( container: ContainerData, player: Player , holder: ItemHolder, destination: Inventory, quantity: number? ) → TransferResult Take, gated on range and on the container being open to that player. The gate lives here because it is the authority check: a client asking to take something is not trusted about where it is standing, nor about whether it ever opened the container.

searchDocs.title: Deposit​
searchDocs.content: </> ContainerService:Deposit( container: ContainerData, holder: ItemHolder, quantity: number? ) → TransferResult Put quantity from holder into the container. The mirror of Take, and the reason a drop pile works: a container is just an inventory, so depositing is the same transfer in the other direction.

searchDocs.title: CollectInventories​
searchDocs.content: </> ContainerService:CollectInventories(container: ContainerData) → {Inventory} Every inventory a viewer of this container should be able to see. For an Inventory container that is just its own. For an ItemGroup it is its own plus the inventory nested inside each slot -- a pile of backpacks shows the backpacks' contents, not the backpacks. The old version did this walk inline in OpenContainer, and again in a slot-change handler, and again in CloseContainer to undo it. Nesting is tracked by holder id now, so it is one function with one caller per event.

searchDocs.title: Open​
searchDocs.content: </> ContainerService:Open( container: ContainerData, player: Player ) → {Inventory}? Open the container for a player. Returns the inventories to expose, or nil when the open was refused -- disabled, locked, or out of range. Note what it does NOT do: attach anything to the player. OnContainerOpened plus this return value is the whole protocol, so the replication layer decides what reaches the client.

searchDocs.title: Close​
searchDocs.content: </> ContainerService:Close( container: ContainerData, player: Player ) → {Inventory} Close the container for a player. Safe to call for a player that never had it open -- the old version had to run its listener cleanup in that case anyway, because a vanished client left connections behind. There are no per-viewer connections now, so there is nothing to leak.

searchDocs.title: ResolveEquipType​
searchDocs.content: </> EquipmentService:ResolveEquipType( equipment: Equipment, config: ItemConfig, preferred: EquipmentType?, first_open: boolean? ) → EquipmentType? Which slot this item should go in. preferred wins when the item allows it, first_open then falls back to the first ALLOWED type whose slot is free, otherwise the item's own declared type. Pure -- it reads the equipment but changes nothing, so a caller can ask "where would this land" without committing to it. The old Equip inlined this logic after it had already begun mutating.

searchDocs.content: </> EquipmentService:Unequip( equipment: Equipment, equip_type: string ) → ItemStack? Take whatever is in a slot back out, and hand it to the caller. The old Unequip decided for itself: task.defer an AddItem, and Drop if that failed. Both of those are placement decisions the caller is better placed to make -- and doing them deferred meant a failure surfaced nowhere.

searchDocs.title: Swap​
searchDocs.content: </> EquipmentService:Swap( equipment: Equipment, from_type: string, to_type: string ) → boolean Exchange two equip slots. Refuses unless BOTH occupants may live in the other's slot. Every check runs before the first write, so a refusal cannot leave one side moved -- the old Swap had three separate mutate-then-fire branches, one of which fired OnUpdate and two of which did not.

searchDocs.content: </> EquipmentService:Clear(equipment: Equipment) → {ItemStack} Empties every slot and returns the contents. The old Clear spawned an item:Unequip per item on a separate thread and returned the items anyway, so callers raced it.

searchDocs.content: </> GroundItemService:FindMergeable( stack: ItemStack, position: Vector3 ) → GroundSpawn? A pile in the same cell that stack could merge into. Merge eligibility is HolderService:AreMergeable, which compares durability and skin as well as class. The old service compared ClassName alone and additionally refused to merge anything whose MaxQuantity was 1, so a damaged rifle could absorb a pristine one. This is stricter, and it is the rule the rest of the model already uses -- see the merge-strictness open question in src2/PORT.md.

searchDocs.content: </> GroundItemService:Place( holder: ItemHolder, cframe: CFrame , options: DropOptions? ) → GroundSpawn? Put an existing ground holder into the world at cframe. The holder must already hold a stack. Use this when something has produced a pile and needs it placed -- InventoryService:Drop returns exactly that.

searchDocs.title: PlaceStack​
searchDocs.content: </> GroundItemService:PlaceStack( stack: ItemStack, cframe: CFrame , options: DropOptions? ) → GroundSpawn? Place a loose stack, with no source holder. This is how a spawner, a loot table or an NPC death drop puts something on the ground: there is no holder it is coming out of, so one is created for it.

searchDocs.title: Drop​
searchDocs.content: </> GroundItemService:Drop( holder: ItemHolder, cframe: CFrame , quantity: number?, options: DropOptions? ) → GroundSpawn? Drop quantity out of holder onto the ground. holder is wherever the quantity is coming from -- an inventory slot, an equipment slot, another pile. It is NOT emptied unless the whole stack moves, and it is never cleared as a side effect: an emptied slot is just an empty slot, and the caller does not have to know which of those happened. Returns the pile the quantity landed in, which may be one that already existed.

searchDocs.title: Take​
searchDocs.content: </> GroundItemService:Take( spawn: GroundSpawn, inventory: Inventory, quantity: number? ) → TransferResult Move quantity from a pile into an inventory. Returns what actually moved. A pile that empties is removed; one that does not is left exactly as it is, holding the remainder -- which is the case the old model could not express, because the thing holding the excess was the item being taken.

searchDocs.content: </> GroundSpawnerService:Spawn(spawner: GroundSpawnerData) → boolean Roll and place this spawner's loot. Returns whether anything was placed. searchDocs.title: Advance​
searchDocs.content: </> GroundSpawnerService:Advance() → number Run one pass over the respawn queue. A spawner that spawns leaves the queue; one that could not -- a player stood nearby, or its table rolled empty -- stays for the next pass. Returns how many spawned. The old version rebuilt the queue array each pass and iterated the previous one. Doing it against a set means a spawner modified DURING a pass is still queued at the end of it, rather than being dropped because it was not in the array the pass started with.

searchDocs.content: </> HolderService:CreateGround(stack: ItemStack?) → ItemHolder A world pile. Gets a bare CUID: a ground pile has no owner, so there is nothing to derive an id from. Unlimited by default -- the ground has no stack limit.

searchDocs.title: CreateSlot​
searchDocs.content: </> HolderService:CreateSlot( owner_id: string, slot_key: string | number, max_quantity: number?, accepts: ((config: ItemConfig) → boolean)? ) → ItemHolder A slot inside something. The id is DERIVED: {owner_id}_{slot_key}. For an inventory the key is the slot's allocation index; for equipment it is the equip type, which reads straight off the wire (aB3f_Primary). Either way the id is reproducible from facts both realms already have, so replicating a slot costs the key rather than an opaque string. max_quantity nil means unlimited -- that is the replacement for threading unlimited_stack through every call.

searchDocs.title: GetNetworkSerialized​
searchDocs.content: </> InventoryService:GetNetworkSerialized(inventory: Inventory) → Types.NetworkInventory Wire payload for one inventory. See Types.NetworkInventory for why the shape lives there rather than in the route module. THREE ARRAYS, NOT ONE RECORD PER SLOT Slots every live slot number, in order. Position in this array is the slot's position, and the client derives its id as{Id}_{Number}. Sending the numbers -- rather than a count -- is what makes slot add/remove replicable, since numbers are never reused and so have gaps. LimitOverrides only slots whose limit differs from SlotLimit. Contents only slots that hold something. One record per slot was the obvious shape and the wrong one: BufferNet spends a whole byte on every Optional presence flag, so a 30-slot bag with 10 items spent ~210 bytes saying "empty" 20 times over. Splitting the arrays roughly halves the payload without touching the transport. NOT REPRESENTED: a holder's Accepts predicate. It is a function, so no wire format can carry it -- the client has to reconstruct slot filters from the inventory's own definition.

searchDocs.title: AdjustedThreshold​
searchDocs.content: </> ItemSpawnData:AdjustedThreshold( threshold: number, emptiness_modifier: number?, server_modifier: number? ) → number The emptiness threshold actually applied, after server fullness. Exposed because it is the one piece of arithmetic here worth asserting directly, and because its direction is easy to get backwards. With an explicit EmptinessModifier the threshold is simply scaled. Without one it runs the original's curve, where server_modifier is 1 on an EMPTY server and falls toward 0.5 as it fills. The curve turns that into a LOWER effective threshold, so a busy server spawns MORE -- and past a point it goes negative, meaning the emptiness check can never fire at all. Preserved as it was. Whether that is the intended behaviour is a question for whoever owns the loot economy, but it is not a porting decision.

searchDocs.title: Commit​
searchDocs.content: </> TransactionService:Commit(tx: Transaction) → ( boolean, string? ) Applies every shadow at once. searchDocs.title: The problem it exists to fix​
searchDocs.content: In the old model, quantity lives on the item object, and an item object can only be in one place. A partial move therefore has to either clamp the quantity or destroy the item at zero — BaseItem:SetQuantity does both:  self.Quantity = math.clamp(quantity, 0, max_stack) local remainder = math.abs(quantity - self.Quantity) if (self.Quantity <= 0) then self:Destroy() end   Pick up a ground pile of 5,000 with room for 200 and the other 4,800 have nowhere to live, because the thing that held them was the item.

searchDocs.title: The model​
searchDocs.content: ItemStack	a quantity of one item kind. Pure data, owns no location. ItemHolder	a place a stack can sit — ground pile, inventory slot, equip slot. Holds at most one stack.  Ground piles and slots become the same type, differing only in their capacity rule. A transfer moves quantity between stacks; whatever will not fit stays where it was, because the source holder still exists and still holds it.  Every operation preserves one invariant:  total quantity before == total quantity after

searchDocs.title: Where to start​
searchDocs.content: HolderService — the conservation layer. Everything else is built on Transfer.InventoryService — what holders mean: nesting, weight rollup, save/load.TransactionService — staged changes that apply all-or-nothing.ItemService — item registries and instance state.
